title: Escalation, handover and speaking up
blurb: Escalate clearly with SBAR, keep going up the chain when a concern is not acted on, use fresh eyes on fetal monitoring, and raise concerns about public protection the right way.
question: A midwife thinks a woman's CTG has become pathological. The obstetric registrar reviews it by phone, says it is fine and declines to attend. The midwife is still concerned. What should she do?

teach.body: SPM 5.6 asks midwives to recognise risks to public protection and quality of care and to escalate concerns in line with local and national escalation guidance. Code 16 says act without delay if there is a risk to patient safety, and 16.1 says raise and, if necessary, escalate any concerns. Code 13.3 says ask for help when something is beyond your competence. In plain English: if you are worried, say so clearly, and keep going up until someone acts.

letters.word: Situation: who you are, who, what now
Assessment: what you think is happening
Recommendation: what you need, by when

teach.caption: NHS England SBAR communication tool. It works for handover and for urgent calls.

teach.body: S: 'This is Ruth, labour ward room 4. Jo, 39 weeks, has a CTG I think is pathological.' B: 'She is 7 cm, on oxytocin, with meconium-stained liquor.' A: 'For 40 minutes there have been late decelerations with reduced variability; fresh eyes from the coordinator agree.' R: 'I need you to review her in person now.' The registrar declines. Ruth tells the coordinator and they call the consultant on call, recording each call and response.

teach.h: When a concern is not acted on

steps.label: Still worried?
steps.sub: Say so; ask for review in person

teach.caption: Code 9.3: deal with differences of professional opinion by discussion and informed debate; a safety concern is still escalated (Code 16.1).

teach.body: Saving Babies' Lives v3 element 4 asks for a structured, systematic review of fetal monitoring with 'fresh eyes' from another clinician: at least hourly when a CTG is in use, and at least every four hours with intermittent auscultation. Fresh eyes counter the human tendency to normalise a slowly worsening trace. Staff also need an annual fetal monitoring competency assessment.

head: Red flag
Threshold
teach.caption: Notify the midwife in charge, who decides whether staffing is the cause and what to do. Record every red flag.
Keep a written record. Giving your name makes the concern easier to investigate and gives the best legal protection.

teach.body: Some concerns are about a colleague or the service, not one woman: a colleague who seems unfit to practise, falsified records, unsafe staffing. Support colleagues (Code 8.7), but never at the expense of safety: act on an immediate risk by telling the person in charge now. Do not obstruct or victimise anyone who raises a concern (Code 16.5). Local Freedom to Speak Up Guardians remain available.
teach.cite: NMC Code 8.7, 16.1, 16.5; NMC Raising concerns guidance

teach.text: Escalation is not finished when you have told one person. If the response does not match your concern, go to the next level, and document each step. Equally, the regulator is not the first stop for a ward-level concern: start with your line manager unless that is unsafe or ineffective.

items: SBAR: Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation; end with what you need and by when.
If a concern is not acted on, escalate up the chain (coordinator, consultant) and record each step.
Fresh eyes: at least hourly with CTG, at least four-hourly with intermittent auscultation (SBL v3).
NG4 red flags, such as a triage delay of 30 minutes or more, go to the midwife in charge and are recorded.
Raising concerns: line manager, designated person, higher level, then a regulator such as the CQC.

summary: You can now escalate a concern clearly with SBAR and keep going up the chain until it is acted on. You can also apply fresh eyes to fetal monitoring, recognise staffing red flags, and raise a concern about public protection through the right stages.

A.q: In the SBAR communication tool, what does the A stand for?
options: Action
Analysis
Assessment
Allocation

whyNot.0: Action is close to Recommendation, but A is Assessment.
whyNot.1: Analysis is not the SBAR term.
whyNot.3: Allocation is not part of SBAR.

A.q: A woman in established labour has continuous CTG monitoring. How often should a fresh eyes review take place under Saving Babies' Lives v3?
options: At least every 4 hours
At least every hour
At least every 2 hours
At each vaginal examination
A.why: SBL v3 4.4: fresh eyes at least hourly with CTG, at least 4-hourly with intermittent auscultation.

whyNot.0: Four-hourly applies to intermittent auscultation, not CTG.
whyNot.2: Two-hourly is too infrequent for CTG.
whyNot.3: Vaginal examinations are not the trigger for fresh eyes.

A.q: A midwife has a concern about unsafe practice on her ward. According to NMC guidance, who should she normally raise it with first?
options: Her line manager
The Care Quality Commission
The NMC
The trust chief executive
A.why: NMC stages: line manager first (verbally or in writing, keeping a record), then a designated person, then a higher level, then a regulator.

whyNot.1: The CQC is a later stage, a regulator.
whyNot.2: The NMC regulates registrants; it is not the first stop for a ward concern.
whyNot.3: The chief executive is a higher level, used if earlier stages fail.

B.q: A midwife calls the registrar about a woman with a rising temperature in labour. Which statement is the Recommendation part of SBAR?
options: 'Her temperature is 38.3 °C and pulse 112.'
'She has had ruptured membranes for 20 hours.'
'I think she may be developing sepsis.'
'I need you to review her within 15 minutes.'
B.why: The Recommendation states what you need and by when.

whyNot.0: Observations belong to the Assessment (or Situation).
whyNot.2: Your clinical judgement is the Assessment.

B.q: The registrar reviews a CTG by phone, says it is normal and declines to attend. The midwife and the coordinator both think it is pathological. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Repeat the call to the registrar in an hour
Escalate to the consultant obstetrician on call
Document the disagreement and continue to observe
Ask the woman whether she wants a review
B.why: Code 16 (act without delay) and 16.1: raise and, if necessary, escalate concerns. When the response does not address the concern, escalate to the next level in the escalation policy.

whyNot.0: Waiting an hour delays action on a pathological trace.
whyNot.2: Documentation is needed, but continuing to observe leaves the risk unaddressed.
whyNot.3: The woman should be informed, but escalation is the professional's duty.

B.q: On a busy labour ward, a woman waits 40 minutes between arriving and being triaged. What should happen?
options: Record it in her notes at the next review
Ask the woman to make a formal complaint
Notify the midwife in charge as a red flag
Report it to the CQC as a staffing breach
B.why: NICE NG4 box 3: a delay of 30 minutes or more between presentation and triage is a midwifery red flag; the midwife in charge is notified and decides whether staffing is the cause.

whyNot.0: A red flag needs action now, not just a later note.
whyNot.1: The professional duty is to report it, not to ask the woman to complain.
whyNot.3: Red flags are handled and recorded locally by the midwife in charge first.

C.q: A midwife tells her manager that a colleague has twice recorded observations she did not take. A month later nothing has changed and the manager will not discuss it. What should she do next?
options: Raise it with the trust's designated person
Report the colleague to the police
Confront the colleague in front of others
Wait for the annual appraisal
C.why: NMC stages: if the line manager does not act, go to the designated person in the organisation (such as a Freedom to Speak Up Guardian), then a higher level, then a regulator.

whyNot.1: Falsified records are a professional and organisational matter first, not a police one.
whyNot.2: Public confrontation is unprofessional and does not escalate the concern.

C.q: A low-risk woman is labouring in a midwife-led unit with intermittent auscultation. How often should a fresh eyes review take place?
options: At least every hour
At least every 2 hours
At least every 4 hours
Once in the second stage
C.why: SBL v3 4.4: fresh eyes at least every 4 hours with intermittent auscultation, and at least hourly with CTG.

whyNot.1: Two-hourly is not the SBL v3 interval.
whyNot.3: One review in the second stage is not the SBL v3 standard.

C.q: A student midwife saw a midwife ignore a woman's request for pain relief for over an hour. She is afraid raising it will harm her placement. What is the most accurate advice?
options: Students should leave concerns to their assessor
She should wait until the placement ends
She should raise it anonymously online
Students are protected and should raise it
C.why: NMC guidance: students have whistleblowing protection (since 6 April 2015). Giving your name makes a concern easier to investigate and gives the best protection.

whyNot.0: Students have their own duty and route to raise concerns.
whyNot.2: Posting online breaches confidentiality and is not a route to raise concerns.

reteach.title: The escalation ladder
reteach.question: What do you do when you have spoken up and nothing happens?

blocks.body: Escalation is a ladder, not a single step. Say it clearly with SBAR and state what you need. If the response does not match the risk, climb to the next rung: coordinator, then consultant. Document each call. For concerns about colleagues or the service, the ladder is line manager, designated person, higher level, regulator.

blocks.text: 'I told the registrar' is not the end of your duty if the woman or baby is still at risk.

explain.body: Situation: who you are, where you are, who the woman is and what is happening now. It tells the listener in seconds why you are calling.

test.q: Which statement belongs in the Situation part of SBAR?
options: 'She had a caesarean birth two years ago.'
'I think this is a placental abruption.'
'Please come and review her in person now.'
'I'm calling about Amy, bleeding in room 2.'
test.why: Situation states who and what is happening now.

explain.body: Code 9.3: deal with differences of professional opinion with colleagues by discussion and informed debate, respecting their views. Code 16 (act without delay) and 16.1 (raise and escalate) still apply where safety is at risk.

test.q: According to the NMC Code, how should a midwife deal with a difference of professional opinion with a colleague?
options: Defer to the more senior colleague
Discuss it with informed debate
Report it to the NMC at once
Record it and take no further action
test.why: Code 9.3: deal with differences of professional opinion by discussion and informed debate, while escalating if safety is at risk.

whyNot.0: Seniority does not override a safety concern.
whyNot.2: A disagreement is not in itself a fitness to practise matter.
whyNot.3: Recording alone does not resolve the difference or any risk.

explain.h: A colleague who may be unsafe
explain.body: Code 8.7: support colleagues with health or performance problems, but never at the expense of patient or public safety. An immediate risk goes to the person in charge now.

rows.label: Tell the person in charge now

test.q: At the start of a night shift a midwife notices her colleague smells strongly of alcohol and is unsteady. What should she do?
options: Cover her workload quietly for the night
Suggest she drinks coffee before starting
Tell the midwife in charge straight away
Raise it at the next team meeting
test.why: Code 8.7 and 16.1: support the colleague but act on an immediate risk to women and babies by informing the person in charge now.

whyNot.0: Covering for her hides a risk to women and babies.
whyNot.1: Coffee does not make her safe to practise.
whyNot.3: A delayed discussion leaves women at risk tonight.

explain.body: If internal routes fail or are unsafe, a concern can go to a regulator or helpline, for example the Care Quality Commission in England. Protect, unions and professional bodies can advise.

test.q: A midwife has raised a serious concern about an English maternity unit through every internal route without response. Which body is an appropriate external regulator to contact?
options: Care Quality Commission
Health and Safety Executive
General Medical Council
Local authority children's services
test.why: NMC guidance gives a regulator such as the CQC in England as the stage after internal routes.

whyNot.1: The HSE regulates workplace health and safety, not the quality of maternity care.
whyNot.2: The GMC regulates doctors, not maternity services.
whyNot.3: Children's services deal with safeguarding, not service quality concerns.
